title: Beyond Anxiety and Depression
objective: After this level you can explain in general terms what ADHD, OCD, PTSD and bipolar disorder are, and why casual labels mislead.
summary: OCD, ADHD, bipolar disorder and PTSD are real conditions with specific features. Borrowing their names for everyday quirks blurs what they involve.

cards.headline: "I'm so OCD about my desk." Is that what OCD is?
cards.body: You've probably heard condition names used as casual labels. What people with OCD actually describe shows why that label misleads.

cards.headline: OCD isn't a love of tidiness
cards.body: In OCD, obsessions are intrusive, unwanted thoughts, urges or images that make most people anxious. Compulsions are repetitive behaviors a person feels driven to do, often in response. People with OCD don't enjoy their compulsions; they get only temporary relief from anxiety. They may spend more than an hour a day on them and can't stop, even knowing it's excessive. A tidy desk you enjoy is a preference. OCD is a loop that costs hours and brings no joy.

items.label: ADHD
points: Frequent, across situations, and getting in the way of daily life

items.label: Bipolar disorder
points: Clear shifts in mood, energy and activity

items.label: PTSD
points: Symptoms that last after a traumatic event
Feeling stressed or frightened even when not in danger

cards.headline: Why casual labels mislead
cards.body: Everyone loses focus sometimes, and ADHD is different because the behaviors are frequent, show up everywhere and interfere with life, often continuing from childhood into adulthood. Trauma doesn't doom anyone to PTSD either: many people have reactions at first, and most recover as those reactions fade. A joke label can't tell these apart. Level 2's psychologists and psychiatrists are the ones trained to diagnose.

cards.headline: Labels, used carefully
learned: OCD: unwanted obsessions and compulsions, no pleasure
ADHD: frequent, interfering inattention or impulsivity
Bipolar disorder: clear shifts between up and down episodes
Most people recover after trauma; PTSD is when symptoms last

questions.prompt: According to NIMH, what do people with OCD get from carrying out their compulsions?

options.label: Real enjoyment, like a favorite hobby
options.rationale: People with OCD don't get pleasure from compulsions.

options.label: A boost in focus and energy

questions.explanation: Compulsions bring no pleasure, only temporary relief from the anxiety that obsessions cause.

questions.prompt: A friend calls herself "so OCD" because she enjoys sorting her books by color. Why does the label mislead?

options.label: OCD is only ever about hand washing
options.rationale: OCD involves many kinds of obsessions and compulsions.

options.label: OCD means unwanted, anxious loops, not enjoyable habits
Anyone who likes order has OCD
options.rationale: Liking order is a preference, not a disorder.

options.label: Sorting books is a sign of bipolar disorder
options.rationale: Bipolar disorder is about shifts in mood and energy.

questions.explanation: OCD involves unwanted obsessions and compulsions that bring no pleasure and can take hours; an enjoyable preference for order is something else.

questions.prompt: Most people who go through trauma recover without PTSD. A researcher studies only people who developed it. Which Level 8 weakness does that echo?

options.label: Self-reports that people bend to look good
options.rationale: The problem here is who gets studied, not how they answer.

options.label: Observers being noticed and changing behavior
Unusual cases that are hard to generalize from
Ethics boards blocking the research
options.rationale: Nothing here suggests the study is blocked.

questions.explanation: Like case studies of rare people, a sample of only those who developed PTSD would miss that most trauma survivors recover.
